reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India national programmes
clinicalPearls: A severe form of dengue, a mosquito-borne flaviviral infection spread by Aedes aegypti, with recurrent large outbreaks across India
The defining features are plasma leakage (haemoconcentration, effusions, ascites), bleeding tendency and thrombocytopenia, which can progress to dengue shock syndrome
The critical, most dangerous period begins around the time of defervescence, when capillary leak peaks, so patients can deteriorate just as fever settles

WHO warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly, fluid accumulation and a rising haematocrit with falling platelets) flag patients at risk of severe disease
Secondary infection with a different dengue serotype increases the risk of severe disease through antibody-dependent enhancement
Management is meticulous fluid balance guided by haematocrit and clinical status; there is no specific antiviral, and both under- and over-resuscitation are harmful
Platelet transfusion is not indicated purely for a low count and should be reserved for significant bleeding
Diagnosis uses NS1 antigen early and IgM/IgG serology or PCR, with serial full blood counts to track haematocrit and platelets
reference.pathophysiology: Following an infective Aedes bite, dengue virus replicates and causes a systemic febrile illness. In severe dengue an intense host immune and cytokine response transiently increases vascular permeability, allowing plasma to leak from the intravascular compartment; this manifests as haemoconcentration, serous effusions and, if severe, hypovolaemic shock. Concurrent thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, coagulopathy and vascular fragility produce the bleeding diathesis. Pre-existing heterotypic antibodies from a prior infection can enhance viral uptake into cells (antibody-dependent enhancement), heightening the risk of severe disease on secondary infection.
additionalDifferentials: Chikungunya and Zika co-circulating arboviral illness
infectionMimics: Acute leukaemia or other causes of thrombocytopenia with bleeding
additionalInvestigations: NS1 antigen in early illness and dengue IgM/IgG serology or RT-PCR
Serial full blood counts monitoring haematocrit and platelet trends
Coagulation profile and liver enzymes to assess severity
Ultrasound to detect plasma leakage (ascites, pleural effusion, gallbladder wall oedema)
Blood grouping and cross-match if significant bleeding occurs
redFlags: WHO warning signs: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, restlessness or lethargy, and clinical fluid accumulation
Rising haematocrit with a rapidly falling platelet count indicating intensifying plasma leak
Signs of shock (narrow pulse pressure, cold clammy peripheries, tachycardia, hypotension) marking dengue shock syndrome
Deterioration around defervescence, the classic timing of the critical phase
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and careful fluid management the great majority recover fully. Untreated or poorly managed severe dengue with prolonged shock or major haemorrhage carries significant mortality, but timely, judicious supportive care dramatically reduces death rates.
pitfalls: Assuming a patient is improving when fever settles, missing the onset of the critical plasma-leak phase
Over-transfusing platelets based on the count alone rather than for clinical bleeding
Excessive intravenous fluids causing fluid overload and respiratory compromise, or inadequate fluids allowing shock
Giving NSAIDs or other agents that worsen bleeding and gastric irritation
